title: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
description: French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.T
body: French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies. "No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers. By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted."The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them."Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe."We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens."Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too."Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing."To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC. "Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.But no formal attribution has been made.None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats. Additional reporting from Chris Vallance

schema.headline: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits

title: Sharp objects found in Halloween sweets in Germany, Austria and Hungary
description: Needles and other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets handed out over Halloween in Germany, Austria and Hungary, prompting police to issue w
body: Needles and other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets handed out over Halloween in Germany, Austria and Hungary, prompting police to issue warnings to parents to check what their children have been given.Police in a number of German states have reported cases, from Bavaria in the south-east to Lower Saxony in the north.A girl aged nine hurt her tongue while eating a chocolate bar in Bremervörde, west of Hamburg. A 5cm-long (2in) pin was then found inside it.Meanwhile, police in Hungary have launched a criminal investigation after nails, screws and pieces of wire were found in sweets handed out to children who had been trick-or-treating in and around the town of Gyömrő, to the east of Budapest.The local authority said one young girl had been handed a toffee with a nail inside a chocolate wrapper and that she had fortunately noticed in time and had not swallowed the sweet.Several cases have also been reported across Austria, where Interior Minister Gerhard Karner condemned the incidents as "cowardly, malicious and in some cases life-threatening".

schema.headline: Sharp objects found in Halloween sweets in Germany, Austria and Hungary

title: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock
description: In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knes
body: In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.That makes them potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government. That person will be given 28 days to do so, with a potential 14-day extension.The president has wide discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition. They do not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.On Wednesday morning, Herzog was presented with the official results by Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg at a ceremony in Jerusalem."In recent days, we have heard voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy. This is a real danger," Sohlberg said."One of the foundations of democracy is the ability to have a peaceful transfer of power. This stems from the understanding that the will of the electorate obligates us all."Herzog announced that he would begin the consultation process on Wednesday evening."In order to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable and good government here for the people of Israel, I expect the factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled," he said.The president also expressed confidence in the Shin Bet's ability to investigate the allegations of foreign interference in the election and appealed for patience.But he warned that Arab Israelis - who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel - "must not be smeared"."I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them toward any community in Israel," he said.Earlier, Sohlberg told a meeting of the Central Elections Committee that the Shin Bet's intelligence appeared to point to a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states", some of which were hostile.It believed further investigation was needed to "connect the dots and determine the scale of the phenomenon with a high degree of certainty", he said.Last week, Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's foreign ministry said it categorically denied the allegation.Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party and an ally of the prime minister, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all the leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified".Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and the prime minister of attempting to "steal the election from the public".On Tuesday, Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and his Likud party were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law".His comments came after Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini - an appointee of the prime minister - to interrogate four Arab politicians, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented.Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying to "obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors".

schema.headline: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock

title: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
description: The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukr
body: The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, as shocked local residents stare at the rubble.Severely damaged buildings are also seen.A voice of a military official is then heard on a two-way radio warning police on the ground of more glide bombs being launched towards Kamyshuvakha."Quickly [go] to the shelter!" one of the police officers tells local residents, who are seen walking into the shelter - at least two floors underground.Seconds later the shelter is hit, and the recording stops. Ukraine said the shelter was near a local school, which was being used to distribute humanitarian aid.BBC Verify has confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the Ukrainian state emergencies service DSNS showing the aftermath Monday's attack in Komyshuvakha.In a post on social media on Wednesday, Zelensky said that "nine aerial bombs were dropped by the Russians. "First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene."The Ukrainian president added that "unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack", describing it as yet another of "thousands" of war crimes committed by Russia.Ukraine's DSNS earlier posted another video showing a huge crater left after the attack on Kamyshuvakha.The Russian military has not publicly commented.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.In a separate development on Wednesday, Zelensky said he talked "in great detail for an hour-and-a-half" with US President Donald Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US on 10-11 November in Abu-Dhabi.The Ukrainian leader - who is currently making a surprise visit to Spain - also said his team had a separate "meaningful" meeting in Brussels with representatives from the US, the EU, France, Britain, Germany, as well as Nato and the World Bank about "post-war reconstruction".He added that the meeting in Belgium's capital would continue on Thursday to discuss "security guarantees" for Ukraine.Since the trilateral talks aimed at ending the war were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.Analysts expect no major breakthrough when the talks resume in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.  Additional reporting Paul Brown, BBC Verify

schema.headline: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing

title: Rafael Nadal: Tennis legend set to join Real Madrid board of directors
description: Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and
body: Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and helped Spain claim five Davis Cups before retiring in 2024.Real's members will be asked to approve the 40-year-old's appointment to the board at a meeting later this month.In a statement announcing the move, external, the club said Nadal was "one of the greatest legends in the history of sport and one of the most admired and recognised Spanish athletes in the world"."It is a great source of pride that a figure of his sporting and human stature, a benchmark of Spanish and world sport, will become part of our board of directors and contribute, from this position of responsibility, to the present and future of our club," Real added.The tennis legend - a boyhood Real fan who holds member's number 67,778 - included a photo of himself as a child in a club kit in his response to the news."I want to thank president Florentino Perez and the board for proposing that I join the board of directors of Real Madrid," Nadal said in his post on X, external."I have accepted this proposal with great excitement, a desire to learn, and a willingness to contribute everything I can."It is currently unclear as to what responsibilities Nadal would hold on the club's board.Perez was re-elected to serve a new four-year term as Real president in June, having held the office since 2009.He swiftly appointed Jose Mourinho to a second spell as head coach, hoping to improve the club's fortunes after they went a second season without a trophy in La Liga, the Champions League or the Copa del Rey.Real are currently third in the league after 11 games - three points behind defending champions Barcelona.

schema.headline: Rafael Nadal: Tennis legend set to join Real Madrid board of directors

title: Abdul El-Sayed, Melat Kiros, Adrian Boafo: The politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
description: "JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.Abdul El-Sayed,
body: "JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations."My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests. Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House. Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

schema.headline: Abdul El-Sayed, Melat Kiros, Adrian Boafo: The politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms

title: Air pollution: Indian capital Delhi's air quality worsens ahead of Diwali festival
description: Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.The city
body: Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, northwesterly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external Twitter, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: Air pollution: Indian capital Delhi's air quality worsens ahead of Diwali festival

title: Hungary opens secret police files, 37 years after fall of communism
description: Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itsel
body: Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule. Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members. The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution."I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity,"  Prime Minister Péter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest."Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer. Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided. Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary. Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.Krisztian Ungváry, a historian who has long campaigned for full public access to the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power."In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna Borvendég, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party. Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

schema.headline: Hungary opens secret police files, 37 years after fall of communism

title: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted 'no to war'
description: Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans voted "NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a stu
body: Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans voted "NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a stunning defeat in the midterm elections."We endorse this message," parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X."If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," he warned.Trump acknowledged on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in petrol prices. But he insisted that he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran in February.In an interview with Fox News, Trump said of the midterm results: "I think a part of it was Iran".He went on to say: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."Speaking separately to the BBC's US news partner, CBS News, Trump said the conflict would end "when I say it ends".In recent weeks, Trump has warned that the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei - who has not been seen in public since he was reportedly seriously wounded in the same Israeli air strike on the first day of the war that killed his father and predecessor, Ali - said he did not expect US policy to change. Khamenei released a statement saying anyone who thought there would be any change from American "hostility towards the Iranian nation" was "gravely mistaken". He also said the war would have "much wider dimensions" if it resumed.In a separate development on Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.The IRGC said two of the vessels were still burning, and two additional tankers had been intercepted, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. It said they were trying to travel through a prohibited southern route in the Strait of Hormuz.BBC Verify has been investigating the IRGC claims, and has not found any evidence that four tankers were destroyed. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre said a tanker was struck by two unknown projectiles about 14 nautical miles (26km) north-east of Limah, in Oman's Musandam peninsula, on Tuesday evening. No casualties were reported, it added.On Monday, an Indian crew member of a dhow - a wooden sailing boat - was killed in an attack north-east of Limah. Thirteen other crew members were rescued by Omani authorities.The IRCG also reported on Wednesday that its forces had shot down another US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz.It made a similar claim on Monday night, when US officials said the US military had carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.In an interview with the Financial Times ahead of the midterms, Trump suggested he was happy with the state of the conflict, and that he did not consider them to be "really in a war".When asked about what the newspaper described as "strong hints" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be an attack on Iran this week, Trump said they were "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".Indirect talks to end the conflict have been stalled for months.President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained on Tuesday that his government had been trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue"."No-one will benefit from this war" if it were to resume, he warned.He also emphasised that Iran's supreme leader had granted the government powers to negotiate "issues that he had previously considered off-limits".Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqai said on Monday that the basis of the current indirect negotiations mediated by Qatar remained a seven-step proposal that Iran submitted in September. But he added that the proposal had been "condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days".The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the Strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Additional reporting by Gabriela Pomeroy

schema.headline: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted 'no to war'

title: Rwanda's army team removed from BAL after US sanctions, NBA says
description: The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in
body: The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March. The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.The BBC has asked Rwanda for comment.In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda."What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked. Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports. The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba. It is a professional league featuring 12 club teams from across the continent.Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

schema.headline: Rwanda's army team removed from BAL after US sanctions, NBA says

title: US midterm results a 'victory' for Canadians hopeful of tariff relief
description: It was the midterm result that many in Canada had hoped for - a Democratic sweep that was in part a repudiation by American voters of Donald Trump's t
body: It was the midterm result that many in Canada had hoped for - a Democratic sweep that was in part a repudiation by American voters of Donald Trump's tariff on close trade allies."I was doing cartwheels down the street," said Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Wednesday morning, calling it "a victory for Canada". Tuesday night's result is unlikely to grant Canada relief from those tariffs any time soon, but there is anticipation that the political shifts could create a more favourable environment for Ottawa to get the best deal now that on-again-off-again trade talks are back on.US voters cited affordability as a main concern heading into the midterms and a survey by the Cato Institute in September, external suggested that about 75% believe the tariffs have raised prices.In states like Maine and Michigan, tariffs played a significant role in the hard-fought races.In Maine, incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins clashed with the White House over tariffs.She successfully lobbied to have some duties that directly affected the state removed, including on road salt, refrigeration equipment and seaweed, but in the end lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.A similar story played out in Michigan, where state's the automobile manufacturing industry is deeply intertwined with Canada's - and where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.There are currently several layers of tariffs on Canada, notably on sectors like autos, steel, aluminium and forestry.After trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed in August, the Trump administration imposed an additional 50% tariff on $20bn (£15bn) worth of various Canadian goods, from dairy to cosmetics and furniture.The US also declared a total import ban on motorcycles, whey protein and alcohol.Canada retaliated by slapping the US with its own 50% "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs. Most provinces have also banned the sale of US alcohol in retaliation.Trump had also previously threatened to escalate the trade war with Canada further by ⁠raising tariffs on sectors, including auto manufacturing, as of 1 January.There were signs that his administration had become more sensitive to the optics of its tariffs on Canada in the run up to the election.Just a few days before the vote, Trump told reporters that a trade deal is "very close" after speaking with Prime Minister Mark Carney.Speaking to reporters on Tuesday evening, Carney said of US negotiators that "they're asking less and they're offering more" in recent discussions.On Wednesday, US-Canada Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the midterm results won't change anything in the short term, and dismissed speculation over  what the new Congress might do when they're seated in the new year as "an interesting discussion at a faculty club luncheon". "Our approach will not change and we don't intend to speculate on the approach being taken by the Americans," he said.Pierre Poilievre, leader of Canada's Conservatives, said on Wednesday that "nobody controls Donald Trump". But he said that midterms results show Canada has "massive leverage" given that the tariffs are broadly unpopular. "We've got to use that goodwill to pressure for tariff-free trade," he said. Trump may indeed feel more pressure to sign a deal with Canada now that American voters have clearly communicated their frustration, said Colin Robertson, a former Canadian diplomat and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute."Will this change Trump's mind? It might, because he suffered such a beating at the polls."But he added it remains to be seen how Trump will react from the bruising midterm loss.Canada has an ideal window between now and January - when the new Democratic lawmakers are sworn in - to finalise a deal, Robertson noted.After that, Trump is likely to be distracted by investigations launched by Democrats into Trump's family and finances and some members of his administration, Robertson said.US trade representative Jamieson Greer also said earlier this year that he had ambitions to have interim deals in place with Canada and Mexico around the North American free trade deal, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada, before the end of the year.And while Carney struck a more optimistic tone in recent days on the current state of Canada-US trade talks, he also told Politico last month that he was prepared to wait for a new American president if necessary to reach a deal with the US.

schema.headline: US midterm results a 'victory' for Canadians hopeful of tariff relief

title: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono experiencing 'most difficult days of my life'
description: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.Ten
body: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally"."These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement."I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened."I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him."I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing."Rest in peace, Jesus."Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone."In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time on Monday when the incident occurred.Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him, before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player."As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell"."Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the club statement.Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

schema.headline: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono experiencing 'most difficult days of my life'

title: South Africa local elections: ANC under pressure to reverse decline
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 500 parties are contesting the electionsByKhanyisile NgcoboReporting fromJohannesburgUpdate
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 500 parties are contesting the electionsByKhanyisile NgcoboReporting fromJohannesburgUpdated 9 hours agoSouth Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes. Election officials say voting is going smoothly, despite long queues at some polling stations.Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral."What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.Image source, Khanyisile Ngcobo/BBCImage caption, Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his voteWe found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change."We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of declineThe BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision."It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity. "Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention". "If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.Melanie VerwoerdThe expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever doneOf South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.But that might change.Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC."And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.Image source, Khanyisile Ngcobo/BBCImage caption, Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the yearsVerwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros."We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

schema.headline: South Africa local elections: ANC under pressure to reverse decline

title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night
description: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByNorth America correspondentUpdated 06:53 GMTDemocrats have torn up Donald Trump'
body: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByNorth America correspondentUpdated 06:53 GMTDemocrats have torn up Donald Trump's political map on a night that will send shockwaves through American politics for years to come.With a string of major Senate victories in states that have been reliably Republican for decades - and in Kansas's case, nearly a century - a blue tidal wave crashed across the nation, sweeping Republicans out of power.Halfway through President Donald Trump's second term, the Democrats now have decisive control of the House of Representatives and have wrested a majority back in the Senate. They will be able to frustrate Trump's agenda, and launch investigations into his administration. A historic third impeachment attempt could also be on the cards.Few imagined such an outcome was possible in the months after Trump returned to the White House with unified Republican control of Congress in January 2025. As the public mood turned against him and his party, Democrats had hopes of retaking the House.But they contemplated a Senate map that appeared unfriendly, populated by states Trump had won comfortably just two years ago.Instead, Democrats rewrote the political equations with victories in Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina.In comments to the BBC's US partner CBS, Trump pledged to strike deals with congressional Democrats, adding that he didn't want to have to spend his final two years in office rejecting their legislation.He somewhat undermined that sentiment later, posting a picture to Truth Social of his trademark red baseball hat with the word "veto" emblazoned on it.The president went on to note that his name wasn't on the ballot this year, but if it had been Republicans would have won a decisive victory. Trump had helped elevate many of those Republican candidates, however, and had urged voters to pretend he was up for re-election.LIVE: Follow latest updatesREACTION: Trump accepts Democrats did a 'good job' in electionTHE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key resultsGUIDE: What are the US midterms?In the Senate, Democrats flipped at least six seats, comfortably securing a majority.Adam Hamilton won in Kansas - a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate almost 100 years ago during the Great Depression.James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race, ending a 38-year Democratic losing streak in statewide elections there.In South Carolina, Annie Andrews beat Darline Graham, who had been appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham. Few analysts had that seat in play even a few months ago.Five-term Republican Susan Collins conceded Maine's Senate election to Democrat Troy Jackson.Paralympian Josh Turek flipped the Iowa Senate seat held by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Democrats also wrested from Republicans a Senate seat in Ohio, with Sherrod Brown's comeback victory over Jon Husted.Meanwhile, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has beaten Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's bitterly fought Senate race.Nor was that the end of the electoral carnage for Republicans. Ruby-red Texas witnessed another seismic result in the governor's race.Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, who was earlier this year seen as the prohibitive favourite.Democrats also took governors' races in Iowa, Ohio and Georgia, which made history by electing the first black woman to such a post.Meanwhile, the party has won a House majority for the first time since 2022.They are projected to win 245 House seats and the Republicans 166 seats.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democrats celebrate in Maine where the party won a crucial Senate raceA look at the key races offers plenty of reasons why.Democrats flipped House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Kentucky and Colorado, among others. And they were poised to make gains in Virginia and Indiana. Black Democrats in the southern states turned out in record number, helping to carry their party to victory. And Hispanic voters, whose support had helped secure Trump's presidential victory in 2024, swung decisively back to the Democrats.Democrats won all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border. And Hispanic voters helped Democrats hold House seats in Florida that the state's Republicans had sought to flip by redrawing the congressional district lines.In fact, the congressional redistricting battles that had dominated headlines for months last year ended up being a bust for the Republicans. In Texas, they had hoped their line-drawing would net five new seats for their party. But on Tuesday they may end up losing one seat.If there is a silver lining for conservatives, Florida as a whole still appears to tilt to the right.Republican Senator Ashley Moody narrowly won re-election, as did congressman Byron Donalds, who was elected the Sunshine State's first black governor. And embattled Republicans were able to hold governorships in Vermont and New Hampshire. But the bright spots were few and far between.Just two years ago, Trump won the presidency with 48% of the vote. He claimed an electoral mandate. He then went about governing like it, pushing sometimes unpopular policies on trade and immigration, and launching an Iran war that is opposed by most of the American public.On Tuesday, voters gave him the kind of stinging rebuke that will not be easily forgotten.Figure caption, BBC asks voters across US what brought them to the polls todayFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night

title: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
description: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByDaniel BushWashington correspondentInside the Republican Party, initial shock
body: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByDaniel BushWashington correspondentInside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress."It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power. But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington."It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November."There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".LIVE UPDATES: All the latest developmentsBOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroadRESULTS: How America voted in maps and chartsEXPLAINER: Five reasons why Trump did so badlyZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for nowREACTION: Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms 'disaster'NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inboxThe BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda. The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The result amounted to a rejection of Trump, one top Republican lobbyist said"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats."I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican Senator Jon Husted at an election event in Ohio, where the Senate seat flipped in favour of Democrat Sherrod BrownSince 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."Figure caption, Democrats 'got their wish': Voters react to midterm resultsOthers defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel."He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina."That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican supporters at a watch party in Iowa, where Democrat candidate Josh Turek won a Senate seat Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election. Trump was consumed by the war with Iran abroad and his construction overhaul of Washington at home. The projects included the under-construction ballroom and a helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, renovations to a local golf course, a proposed memorial arch near Arlington Cemetery and renovations to the Kennedy Center.Events like a UFC match at the White House on Trump's 80th birthday in June created the impression that the president was more interested in feting himself than winning the midterms, several sources said. Trump also repeatedly downplayed the rising costs of gas and often cast the affordability issue as a Democratic hoax.Trump turned his full attention to the election in September at the Republican Party's midterm convention. The event was a gamble: Republicans hadn't held a midterm convention in decades, and it was an open question whether voters would tune in.Trump dominated the convention in Dallas, frustrating Republicans who told the BBC they wanted to highlight the party's midterm candidates. In his rambling keynote speech, Trump pledged to give $5,000 (£3,700) to Americans if Republicans retained control of Congress and raised eyebrows with an endorsement of Paxton which included a lengthy criticism of the candidate's lack of charisma and physical appearance."Obviously, that's never helpful," Robin Armstrong, Texas' Republican National Committeeman, said of Trump's critique of Paxton. "You're not going to stop what President Trump says. We just have to kind of live with that."The convention failed to attract a large television audience, and Democrats were quick to call it a failure. "It backfired for Republicans because nobody paid any attention to it," said Terri Burke, the Texas Democratic Party's executive director.Trump's penchant for straying off-message continued when he hit the campaign trail in the final weeks before Election Day. He made headlines for praising Ohio Republican Senator John Husted's physique, and drew criticism for calling Abdul El-Sayed a "jihadist" in the Michigan Senate race.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mike Rogers in Michigan was among the other losing candidates - having been beaten to a Senate seat by Democrat Abdul El-SayedAs Trump criss-crossed the country stumping for Republican candidates, the White House contended with controversies in Washington. Katie Zacharia was ousted after just five days as White House press secretary, and Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the US ambassador to Greece after reports surfaced that she asked a donor to pay her credit card debt.Trump also faced a backlash in October for striking a deal to buy Russian diesel. The agreement, which blindsided members of Congress and drew condemnation from some Republicans, came just weeks after Trump signed a sanctions bill aimed at cutting off Russian oil and gas revenue.Democrats used the deal and other scandals swirling around the White House to make the case for retaking control of Congress. The messaging resonated in the end, as Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress in convincing fashion.A second White House ally said that the president's political aides projected optimism until the final days of the election, even as it became clear the party was headed to defeat.Now, as Republicans take stock of the loss, several said they were ready to look ahead to the 2028 election."Whether that's JD Vance, or Marco Rubio, or Ted Cruz, we've got a pretty big bench," said Scheffler, the state's RNC member. "It'll be a wide open race."Peppin, the Republican strategist, said the midterms results demonstrated the party needed a new direction. "I sincerely hope that we've turned the page from the Trump era, and that we'll have new players, new issues and a new focus moving forward."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton was defeated by Democrat James Talarico in Texas

schema.headline: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
